c.tagline: A volcanic Cycladic island crowned by whitewashed clifftop villages overlooking a dramatic caldera

card: Widely accepted; cash useful for small shops and beach tavernas

taxi.fare: Metered, though scarce and often booked well in advance
taxi.fareNote: Taxis are limited on the island; renting a car or ATV is the more common way to get around

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-style emergency number that connects to police, fire, and ambulance

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: Fira and Oia's clifftop lanes are walkable but very hilly with many stairs; getting between villages requires a bus, car, or ATV

safety.safety: Very safe island, extremely crowded with day-trippers and cruise passengers in peak season
safety.crime: Petty theft in crowded sunset-viewing spots is the main concern

hood_landmark.Fira: Fira's clifftop caldera-edge walkway and cable car
hood_landmark.Oia: Oia's iconic blue-domed churches and sunset viewpoint
hood_landmark.Imerovigli: Imerovigli's Skaros Rock and quieter caldera views
hood_landmark.Akrotiri: The Akrotiri archaeological site, a Bronze Age town preserved in volcanic ash
hood_landmark.Kamari / Perissa: Kamari and Perissa's black volcanic-sand beaches

avoid.reason: Watch belongings in the dense Oia sunset and Fira crowds, and take care on unlit caldera-edge paths at night.

hood_desc: The island's capital and busiest town, with the highest concentration of hotels, shops, and restaurants along the caldera rim.
The postcard village at the island's northern tip, famous for its sunset and considered the most romantic (and crowded) base.
A quieter clifftop village between Fira and Oia, offering equally dramatic caldera views with fewer crowds.
The site of Santorini's best-preserved ancient ruins, a Bronze Age settlement buried and preserved by volcanic ash.
The island's main black-sand beach resorts on the southeastern coast, a lower-key, more affordable base than the caldera villages.

water.note: Tap water comes from desalination and is not for drinking — buy bottled.

transit.sys: KTEL local bus network connecting the island's villages
transit.hours: Roughly 7am-11pm, more frequent in peak season
transit.note: Renting an ATV or car is popular given limited taxi availability and the island's spread-out layout

transport.air: Santorini (Thira) National Airport (JTR), about 20 min from Fira, with direct flights from Athens and seasonal international routes
transport.bus: KTEL buses connect the airport, Fira, Oia, and other villages
transport.ferry: Ferries connect to Athens (Piraeus), Mykonos, and other Cycladic islands
transport.car: Rental cars and ATVs are popular; roads are narrow and can be congested in peak season

net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.ap: A Cosmote or Vodafone Greece tourist SIM or eSIM

tip.s: Not obligatory; rounding up is appreciated for guides and tours

food.name: Tomatokeftedes
food.desc: Fritters of the island's tiny, intensely sweet cherry tomatoes mashed with onion and mint, fried crisp and served with tzatziki.

places.name: Metaxi Mas
places.note: Inland taverna locals rate above anything on the caldera; book weeks ahead in summer.

places.name: To Psaraki
places.note: Fish taverna above the marina with a terrace and excellent Santorini starters.

food.name: Fava Santorinis
food.desc: Yellow split peas grown in the island's volcanic soil, cooked down to a silky puree and topped with raw onion, capers and olive oil.

places.name: Metaxi Mas
places.note: Serves fava the classic way and as fava me koukia with capers; portions are generous.

places.name: Nikolas Taverna
places.note: The oldest taverna in Fira, unchanged and unglamorous, doing the island classics.

food.name: White eggplant
food.desc: Santorini's pale, seedless aubergine is sweeter and less bitter than usual, served grilled, in a salad, or baked with tomato.

places.name: Selene
places.note: The island's benchmark restaurant for elevated Santorini cuisine; also runs cooking classes.

places.name: Metaxi Mas
places.note: Cooks it simply with tomato and cheese, which is exactly how it should be eaten.

food.name: Chloro cheese and Santorini salad
food.desc: Fresh, tangy goat's chloro cheese scattered over cherry tomatoes, capers and caper leaves in place of the usual feta.

places.name: Selene
places.note: Sources chloro from the last island producers; the tasting menu explains each ingredient.

places.name: To Psaraki
places.note: Simple, generous salads with island cheese and a sea view over the marina.

food.name: Brantada
food.desc: Salt cod fried in a light batter and served with fierce garlic skordalia, eaten on the island's feast days and all through Lent.

places.name: To Psaraki
places.note: Fish is landed a few metres away; the brantada and skordalia are a house standard.

places.name: Nikolas Taverna
places.note: No-frills traditional cooking in the middle of town, cash only and no reservations.

food.name: Grilled octopus and fresh seafood
food.desc: Sun-dried octopus charred over coals, plus whatever came in that morning, grilled whole and dressed with lemon and oil.

places.name: Ammoudi Fish Tavern
places.note: Tables at the water's edge under the Oia cliffs; walk down the 300 steps and taxi back.

places.name: To Psaraki
places.note: Better value than the caldera fish tavernas and just as fresh.

food.name: Assyrtiko wine
food.desc: Santorini's flagship white, grown in low basket-woven vines against the wind: bone-dry, mineral and searingly citrus.

places.name: Santo Wines
places.note: Cooperative winery with terraced caldera views and flights covering every island style.

places.name: Domaine Sigalas
places.note: Serious estate among the vines with guided tastings and food pairings; reserve ahead.

food.name: Vinsanto
food.desc: Sun-dried Assyrtiko grapes aged for years in barrel into a dark, raisiny dessert wine, the island's oldest export.

places.name: Santo Wines
places.note: Vertical Vinsanto tastings at sunset, the classic Santorini winery experience.

places.name: Venetsanos Winery
places.note: 1947 gravity-fed winery carved into the cliff, with a terrace over the caldera.

landmarks: Oia
Whitewashed cave houses and blue domes spill down the caldera cliff in the village whose sunsets draw applause every single evening.
Fira
Santorini's cliff-edge capital stacks white cubic houses 260 metres above the flooded volcano, linked to its old port by cable car and donkey steps.
Akrotiri Archaeological Site
A Minoan-era town exquisitely preserved under volcanic ash since 1600 BC, complete with multi-storey houses, drainage and famous frescoes.
Fira to Oia Caldera Trail
A ten-kilometre rim-top footpath past Imerovigli and Skaros Rock, delivering the island's most sustained and staggering volcano views.
Red Beach
Crimson volcanic cliffs crumble onto dark sand at this dramatic cove near Akrotiri, Santorini's most photographed stretch of shore.
Amoudi Bay
Below Oia's cliffs, this tiny red-rock harbour serves grilled octopus at water's edge and tempts swimmers to leap from nearby rocks.
Ancient Thera
Hellenistic and Roman ruins straddle a wind-blasted mountain ridge 360 metres up, with dizzying views over both coasts of the island.
Skaros Rock
A headland crag off Imerovigli that once bore the island's medieval capital, now a short scramble rewarded with panoramic caldera solitude.
Pyrgos
The island's former hilltop capital coils around a Venetian castle, offering blue-domed churches and island-wide views without the crowds.
Perissa & Perivolos Black Sand Beach
A long strip of jet-black volcanic sand beneath the Ancient Thera mountain, lined with laid-back beach bars and tavernas.

train.note: There is no railway on Santorini or anywhere in the Cyclades - Hellenic Train's network (https://www.hellenictrain.gr/en) is confined to the Greek mainland, and Greece has no international trains running at all at present. Arrive by ferry or fly into Santorini airport.

bus.note: No international or mainland coach routes exist from an island. KTEL Santorini runs the island network from the Fira central bus station to Oia, Perissa, Kamari, the airport and the ferry port at Athinios, timed loosely around ferry arrivals. Buses are cheap but get packed in July and August; buy tickets from the conductor on board.

intl.to: Piraeus / Athens (Greece) - 5 hr fast ferry or 8 hr conventional
Mykonos, Paros, Naxos & Ios (Greece) - high-speed catamaran

ferry.note: There are no international ferries from Santorini - it is entirely a domestic network, though a busy one. Everything docks at Athinios port on the west coast, below the caldera cliff, with a steep switchback road up to Fira; the old port below Fira takes only cruise tenders. High-speed services run mainly from April to October and are cancelled in strong meltemi winds, which is common in July and August - leave a buffer day before a flight home.

half.name: Ios
half.blurb: A Cycladic island reached by ferry, with a whitewashed hilltop village, sandy beaches, and a laid-back nightlife scene.

half.name: Thirasia
half.blurb: The smaller island fragment across the caldera from Santorini, with two quiet villages and far fewer visitors than the main island.

half.name: Nea Kameni and Palea Kameni
half.blurb: A boat trip to the still-active volcanic islet in the caldera's center, followed by a stop at natural warm-water hot springs.

full.name: Anafi
full.blurb: A remote, sparsely developed island east of Santorini with quiet beaches and a monastery perched on a cliff above the sea.
